trial_name: PATCH-Trauma — Prehospital Tranexamic Acid for Severe Trauma (2023)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: PATCH-Trauma Investigators and the ANZICS Clinical Trials Group. Prehospital Tranexamic Acid for Severe Trauma. N Engl J Med. 2023;389(2):127-136.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pragmatic trial
one_liner: Prehospital tranexamic acid did not improve 6-month favorable functional survival in severe trauma patients, despite lowering early 24-hour and 28-day mortality.

pico.population: Adults (>=18 years) with major trauma at risk of trauma-induced coagulopathy (COAST score >=3) within 3 hours of injury.
pico.intervention: Prehospital IV/IO 1 g TXA bolus over ~10 minutes, followed by 1 g IV infusion over 8 hours in hospital.
pico.comparison: Matching 0.9% sodium chloride placebo bolus and infusion.
pico.outcome: Primary: Survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months (GOS-E score 5-8).

background.existing_knowledge: Trauma-induced coagulopathy and hyperfibrinolysis cause early hemorrhagic death and major morbidity. CRASH-2 showed in-hospital TXA within 3 hours reduced mortality.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether early prehospital TXA administration improves patient-important long-term functional recovery in advanced, modern trauma systems remained uncertain.
background.hypothesis: Prehospital TXA with in-hospital continuation increases survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months compared with placebo in severe trauma.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, investigator-initiated pragmatic trial in Australia, New Zealand, and Germany.
methods.setting: Participating ambulance services and trauma hospitals within advanced trauma systems; enrolled prehospital, continued in hospital.

inclusion: At risk of trauma-induced coagulopathy (COAST score >=3)
Treatment initiation feasible within 3 hours of injury
exclusion: Residence in nursing home or residential aged care facility

methods.intervention: 1 g IV/IO TXA bolus (10 mL) prehospital over ~10 minutes, then 1 g IV infusion in 100 mL over 8 hours upon hospital arrival.
methods.comparison: Matching 0.9% sodium chloride placebo bolus and infusion with identical volume, timing, and packaging.
methods.blinding: Double-blind (prehospital clinicians, hospital staff, patients/surrogates, investigators, outcome assessors).
methods.sample_size_power: 1184 required to detect 9% absolute increase in 6-month favorable GOS-E (60% to 69%) at 90% power, alpha 0.05. Target raised to 1316 for 10% attrition. Enrolment stopped at 1310 due to drug expiry.
methods.primary_outcome: Survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months (GOS-E score 5–8, upper moderate disability to good recovery).
secondary_outcomes: Mortality at 24 hours, 28 days, and 6 months
Cause-specific mortality (bleeding, head injury) at 6 months
Vascular occlusive events to day 28, discharge, or death
Sepsis episodes to day 28, discharge, or death
Red blood cell transfusion units within 24 hours
methods.follow_up: Clinical outcomes to 28 days (or hospital discharge/death); functional outcome at 6 months via structured telephone GOS-E interview.

headline_bullets: Primary functional endpoint (GOS-E 5-8 at 6 months) was identical between TXA and placebo (53.7% vs 53.7%, RR 1.00).
TXA significantly reduced mortality at 24 hours (9.7% vs 14.1%, RR 0.69) and 28 days (17.3% vs 21.8%, RR 0.79).
Vascular occlusive events were not increased with TXA (8.5% vs 9.8%, RR 0.87).
TXA reduced 24-hour transfusion requirements among transfused patients by a median of 1 RBC unit.

outcomes_table.outcome: Survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months (GOS-E 5-8, primary complete-case)
Survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months (multiple imputation)

outcomes_table.note: Includes DVT, PE, MI, stroke, arterial events

outcomes_table.outcome: RBC units transfused within 24 hours (among transfused)

subgroup_table.subgroup: Time to first dose 1 to <2 hours

safety: Vascular occlusive events occurred in 8.5% with TXA vs 9.8% with placebo (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.62–1.22).
Sepsis episodes occurred in 17.4% with TXA vs 18.2% with placebo (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.76–1.20).
No excess of thrombotic or septic complications was observed in the TXA group.

domains.notes: Pre-prepared identical study packs stratified by jurisdiction and baseline GCS (<9 vs >=9).
Double-blind with matched placebo packs maintained across prehospital and in-hospital teams.
ITT population n=1300 (TXA 657, placebo 643). 13% missing 6-month primary outcome (TXA 572, placebo 559 assessed); multiple imputation gave identical results.
Full protocol adherence in 67.3% TXA vs 63.0% placebo; both doses given in 78.4% vs 74.7%. Open-label TXA given in 15.8% vs 16.5%.
Well balanced: mean age 45.4 vs 44.8 years, median ISS 29 vs 29, blunt trauma 91.8% vs 92.4%, GCS <9 in 40.2% vs 38.9%, SBP <=75 mm Hg in 38.4% vs 40.6%.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate due to strong randomization and blinding, offset by 13% missing primary outcomes and ~16% open-label TXA contamination in both arms.

domains.notes: Severely injured adult trauma population (median ISS 29, ~40% GCS <9, ~40% severe hypotension) in advanced EMS systems.
92% blunt trauma in advanced EMS networks; less applicable to penetrating trauma, pediatric trauma, pregnancy, or systems lacking early infusion capabilities.

external_validity.verdict: Highly applicable to adult severe blunt trauma in advanced trauma systems, but less generalizable to penetrating trauma or low-resource systems.

strengths: Large, double-blind, pragmatic RCT extending from prehospital field care into hospital.
Targeted high-risk population using a validated prehospital coagulopathy risk score (COAST >=3).
Patient-centered primary functional outcome (GOS-E at 6 months).
Rigorous pre-specified statistical plan with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses.
limitations: 13% missing primary outcome data at 6 months.
Substantial protocol non-adherence, with only 75-78% receiving both doses.
High open-label TXA contamination (~16% in both arms).
Low proportion of penetrating trauma (<8%), limiting subgroup power.

critical_appraisal.summary: PATCH-Trauma is a well-designed prehospital trial showing that while TXA reduces early 24-hour and 28-day mortality, it does not improve 6-month favorable functional recovery.
strengths: Prehospital double-blind randomization with pragmatic field execution.
Use of patient-centered 6-month disability endpoint rather than short-term survival alone.
weaknesses: Contamination from open-label TXA use in ~16% of controls.
13% loss to follow-up for 6-month primary outcome.

sections.authors_conclusion: In adults with severe trauma at risk of coagulopathy treated in advanced EMS systems, prehospital TXA did not increase survival with favorable functional outcome at 6 months.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Supports early TXA administration to prevent early hemorrhagic death, but clinicians should not expect a shift in overall 6-month functional disability driven by traumatic brain injury.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult major trauma patients at risk of hemorrhage and trauma-induced coagulopathy within 3 hours of injury.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean TXA is ineffective at saving lives early; early mortality was significantly reduced without increasing thrombotic risk.
implementation_caveats: Requires prehospital logistics to administer 1 g bolus over ~10 minutes and ensure follow-up 8-hour 1 g IV infusion in hospital.
Primary outcome in severe blunt trauma is heavily influenced by concurrent TBI recovery.

controversies.notes: GOS-E at 6 months is heavily dominated by TBI, whereas TXA targets fibrinolysis and early bleeding death; this may obscure early lifesaving benefits.

controversies.topic: Neutral primary outcome vs positive early mortality signal
controversies.notes: Significant early mortality reduction at 24h (RR 0.69) and 28d (RR 0.79) was detected in secondary outcomes without multiplicity adjustment.
16% of control patients received open-label TXA, potentially biasing the primary outcome effect towards the null.

context_related_trials.relation: In-hospital RCT showing early TXA reduces 28-day mortality in bleeding trauma; PATCH-Trauma tested prehospital delivery with long-term functional endpoints.
Prehospital TXA RCT in severe trauma which showed overall neutral results but benefit in specific high-risk and early-dosing subgroups.

unresolved_questions: Which specific physiological or biomarker phenotypes (e.g., TEG/ROTEM hyperfibrinolysis) benefit most from prehospital TXA?
Does prehospital TXA improve functional outcomes in pure penetrating hemorrhage without concomitant TBI?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Prehospital TXA reduces early 24-hour and 28-day mortality in severe trauma without thrombotic harm, but does not alter 6-month functional disability.
